case_name: Budhi Lal v State Of Uttarakhand
respondent:
State Of Uttarakhand
Supreme Court of India

26 September 2008
Criminal Appeal No.1537 Of 2008 (Arising Out Of S.L.P. (Crl.) No.1988 Of 2008)
The Judgment was delivered by : Dr. Arijit Pasayat J.
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
Leave granted.
1.  Challenge in this appeal is to the judgment of a Division Bench of the Uttarakhand High Court dismissing the appeal filed by the appellant. In the appeal challenge was to the order of conviction recorded by the learned Sessions Judge, Chamoli in Sessions Trial No.8 of 1986 for offence punishable under Section 302 the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (in short 'IPC'). The appellant was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life.
2.  Prosecution story in brief is that house of Budhi Lal (appellant) is one kilometer away from village abadi in village Airash. facts: The case involves Budhi Lal, who was convicted of murdering his wife Jashu Devi.
Budhi Lal had married twice and had seven children with his second wife.
On August 9, 1985, Jaspal (PW.3) visited the house where Budhi Lal lived with his family.
That night, Budhi Lal allegedly murdered Jashu Devi while she was sleeping.
The next morning, Budhi Lal told the villagers that Jashu Devi had died of pain in her stomach.
An investigation was conducted, and a charge sheet was filed against Budhi Lal.
Budhi Lal pleaded innocence, and a trial was held.
Six witnesses were examined to further the prosecution version.
issues: Whether the evidence of PW.3 should be relied upon
Whether a case under Section 302 IPC was made out
petitioner_arguments: Presence of PW.3 in the house has not been established
In view of the accepted prosecution version, a case under Section 302 IPC is not made out
respondent_arguments: The presence of PW.3 has been clearly established by evidence on record
The accused accepted that he was with the deceased in the night of occurrence and they were sleeping in the same room
court_reasoning: The academic distinction between 'murder' and 'culpable homicide not amounting to murder' has always vexed the Courts.
The safest way of approach to the interpretation and application of these provisions seems to be to keep in focus the keywords used in the various clauses of Sections 299 and 300.
holding: The Trial Court and the High Court were justified in holding the appellant guilty
